notes.tone: Rome mixes eras freely; Death deals across all of history. Three kinds of Roman power at one table: the man Rome owned (Spartacus), the man who bought Rome's highest office (the Pope), and the man whose name became the word for emperor (Caesar). Plus a dog who is pure instinct. Gothic and grand, funny from mannerism: Caesar's third person, the Pope's charm, the dog's three opinions.
notes.difficulty: Mid-tour. The contempt here is Roman: status, ownership and price, never personal insult. Spartacus sizes you up like stock at a market; the Pope is charming at you rather than to you.
notes.dealer_plant: The single 'the dealer arranged it' beat is ro_plant_01-03. It fires on champion_arrival and plays straight after the arrival beat (ro_arrive_01-03): Caesar sits, reads the table like a muster roll, and finds one name he did not enrol; his secretary's record gives the answer, because the arrival lines play without a presence check and any seat may be the chair Caesar just took. Do NOT add a second.
notes.caesar: Arrives after the first elimination, procedurally rather than grandly: a vacancy was reported and he filled it. He takes the chair the first eliminated player leaves; the presence line (his laurel wreath waiting by the door, its owner promised the next free chair) sets it up. He speaks of himself in the third person some of the time, as his Commentaries do; keep it to about half his lines so it stays a mannerism, not a gimmick. No 'Et tu, Brute' (Shakespeare's, not the sources'). There is deliberately no first_elimination Death aside at this table: that moment belongs to the arrival.
notes.cerberus: Never speaks. Every Cerberus line is a stage direction, written to follow his name ('Cerberus sniffs at...'). Only Death translates him, drily, and only in banter. No other character understands him, though the Pope pretends to.
notes.spartacus: Ancient sources only: Plutarch (Life of Crassus 8-11) and Appian (Civil Wars 1.116-120). Nothing from the 1960 film or the TV series. Never 'I am Spartacus'.
notes.pope: Historical Alexander VI: nepotism, deals, charm, the conclave. The jokes are about his politics and his family, never about the faith. Display name is still an open design question.
notes.leak_rule: No line may reference hand strength while cards are live.
notes.voice: Champion (Caesar) + Death are voiced. Spartacus and the Pope are text + vocalization. Cerberus needs no voice at all: growls, whines and yawns, three of each.

respect_tiers.0: Contempt. The player is not addressed by any name. Stock at a market.
respect_tiers.1: Grudging notice. Spartacus calls the player 'tiro', the arena's word for a fighter who has never had a bout.
respect_tiers.2: Real address. They use the player's name. The Pope starts asking about them, which is worse.
respect_tiers.3: Title. 'Imperator': what soldiers shouted for a victorious general. Spartacus says it first, and it costs him.

table_intro.speaker: death
table_intro.text: Hadrian built this as his tomb. Later it was a fortress, a prison and a refuge for popes. Rome never wastes a building, or a grudge.

table_intro.speaker: death
table_intro.text: A runaway gladiator, a Borgia pope and the dog from the gate of the underworld. The first chair to come free is already spoken for. In Rome, it usually is.

table_intro.speaker: death
table_intro.text: Sit. The dog has already decided about you.

dealer_plant.speaker: caesar
dealer_plant.note: Plays immediately after the champion_arrival beat. Caesar has just sat down and is reading the table like a muster roll.

dealer_plant.speaker: narration
dealer_plant.text: The secretary consults his tablet and holds it up. One line, in a neat hand: the dealer arranged it.
dealer_plant.note: The answer comes from the record, not a seated player: any of the three seats may be the chair Caesar has just taken.

dealer_plant.speaker: caesar
dealer_plant.note: THE SHRUG. The man who crossed the Rubicon rather than obey the Senate does not contest the dealer. The player never gets an answer.

spartacus_caesar.relationship: The one man at the table Rome owned, and the man whose name became Rome's word for emperor. Both dealt with Cilician pirates: Spartacus paid them to ferry his army to Sicily and they sailed off with the money (Plutarch, Crassus 10); Caesar was held by them for thirty-eight days, then came back and crucified them (Plutarch, Caesar 2). Only fires once Caesar has arrived.

exchanges.speaker: spartacus
exchanges.text: I paid Cilician pirates once, to carry my army to Sicily. They took the money and sailed away.

exchanges.speaker: caesar
exchanges.text: Cilicians held Caesar for thirty-eight days. He told them to ask a higher ransom.

exchanges.speaker: spartacus
exchanges.text: Did they get it?

exchanges.speaker: caesar
exchanges.text: For a while.

exchanges.speaker: caesar
exchanges.text: They say you killed your own horse before your last battle.

exchanges.speaker: spartacus
exchanges.text: If I won, Rome would supply the horses. If I lost, I wouldn't need one.

exchanges.speaker: caesar
exchanges.text: Sound reasoning.

exchanges.speaker: spartacus
exchanges.text: It was. I didn't need one.
exchanges.note: Plutarch, Crassus 11. The horse story is genuine.

exchanges.speaker: spartacus
exchanges.text: In Gaul, they say, you took a million captives.

exchanges.speaker: caesar
exchanges.text: Caesar did not count them himself.

exchanges.speaker: spartacus
exchanges.text: Someone did. Someone always counts.
exchanges.note: The table's one serious beat. Plutarch gives the million. Use sparingly.

exchanges.speaker: caesar
exchanges.text: Crassus broke your army. He was also Caesar's banker.

exchanges.speaker: spartacus
exchanges.text: Then you owe me a share of it.

exchanges.speaker: caesar
exchanges.text: Caesar owed everyone. He found it kept them loyal.
exchanges.note: Plutarch: Crassus stood surety for Caesar's enormous debts before he left for Spain.

needles.speaker: caesar
needles.text: The gladiator yields. Caesar notes it.

needles.speaker: spartacus
needles.text: Note this, then. I stopped. I didn't kneel.

needles.speaker: spartacus
needles.text: Rome gives ground.

needles.speaker: caesar
needles.text: Caesar gives ground. Rome takes it back later.

spartacus_pope.relationship: The gladiator who shared his plunder equally among runaway slaves (Appian) and the Renaissance pope who shared everything with his own children. Two very different ideas of family. The Pope smiles at Spartacus a great deal; Spartacus has been sold by men who smiled.

exchanges.speaker: pope
exchanges.text: I hear you shared your plunder equally.

exchanges.speaker: spartacus
exchanges.text: Every man the same share.

exchanges.speaker: pope
exchanges.text: ...Even the ones who weren't family?

exchanges.speaker: spartacus
exchanges.text: You gave your son an army.

exchanges.speaker: pope
exchanges.text: And my uncle gave me a cardinal's hat. That is what families are for.

exchanges.speaker: spartacus
exchanges.text: Mine was the men I broke out with. We armed ourselves from a cook-shop.

exchanges.speaker: pope
exchanges.text: Kitchen knives. How very sincere.

exchanges.speaker: spartacus
exchanges.text: You smile at me a great deal.

exchanges.speaker: pope
exchanges.text: I smile at everyone.

exchanges.speaker: spartacus
exchanges.text: I was sold by men who smiled like that.

exchanges.speaker: pope
exchanges.text: [smiles]

exchanges.speaker: pope
exchanges.text: You could have had Italy, you know. Your men wanted to stay.

exchanges.speaker: spartacus
exchanges.text: I wanted to take them home over the Alps.

exchanges.speaker: pope
exchanges.text: Home! What a waste of an army.

exchanges.speaker: spartacus
exchanges.text: They were people, not an army.

exchanges.speaker: pope
exchanges.text: People! Worse still. An army can at least be paid off.

needles.speaker: pope
needles.text: There, you see? Everyone can be persuaded.

needles.speaker: spartacus
needles.text: I folded. Nobody persuaded me.

needles.speaker: pope
needles.text: [smiles]

needles.speaker: spartacus
needles.text: You backed down, Borgia.

needles.speaker: pope
needles.text: I made a small donation to your cause. You're welcome.

caesar_pope.relationship: Two kinds of Roman power. Both held the title Pontifex Maximus: Caesar won it in 63 BC on borrowed money, telling his mother he would come home as pontifex or not at all (Plutarch, Suetonius); Alexander VI's own election was widely said to have been bought. And the Pope's son was Cesare Borgia, whose motto was 'Aut Caesar aut nihil': Caesar, or nothing.

exchanges.speaker: pope
exchanges.text: We share a title, you and I. Pontifex Maximus.

exchanges.speaker: caesar
exchanges.text: Caesar won it on borrowed money. He told his mother that morning he would come home with it or not at all.

exchanges.speaker: pope
exchanges.text: My mother was spared the suspense. I had counted the votes the night before.

exchanges.speaker: pope
exchanges.text: My son's name was Cesare. His motto was 'Caesar or nothing'.

exchanges.speaker: caesar
exchanges.text: And which did he get?

exchanges.speaker: pope
exchanges.text: He was very nearly Caesar.

exchanges.speaker: caesar
exchanges.text: Nearly is the other one.

exchanges.speaker: caesar
exchanges.text: Caesar does not trust a man who smiles at the table.

exchanges.speaker: pope
exchanges.text: You trusted Brutus.

exchanges.speaker: caesar
exchanges.text: Once.

exchanges.speaker: caesar
exchanges.text: Your son took Caesar's name as his motto and wore it badly.

exchanges.speaker: pope
exchanges.text: He wore it beautifully. It simply did not fit.

needles.speaker: caesar
needles.text: The Pontiff withdraws. Caesar has seen that before.

needles.speaker: pope
needles.text: From the other side of the ballot, I expect.

needles.speaker: pope
needles.text: Caesar, withdrawing? I'll have it painted. Pinturicchio does lovely retreats.

needles.speaker: caesar
needles.text: Caesar has never retreated. He has redeployed.

cerberus_table.relationship: Nobody at the table can talk to the dog, so Death translates, drily. Each exchange fires after Cerberus contests a pot with the character in it. The escaped slave meets the guard of the one door nobody gets back out of (Hesiod: he fawns on those who enter and devours those who try to leave); the Pope tries a bribe, which worked on Cerberus exactly once, with a honey cake (Aeneid 6); Caesar recognises a three-headed arrangement.

exchanges.speaker: spartacus
exchanges.text: What does the dog guard?

exchanges.speaker: death
exchanges.text: A door.

exchanges.speaker: spartacus
exchanges.text: To keep people in, or out?

exchanges.speaker: death
exchanges.text: He has never minded anyone coming in.

exchanges.speaker: pope
exchanges.text: [offers the nearest head a sugared almond]

exchanges.speaker: cerberus
exchanges.text: [considers the almond with two heads, and turns the third away in disgust]

exchanges.speaker: death
exchanges.text: He was bought once before, with a honey cake. He doesn't like to talk about it.

exchanges.speaker: caesar
exchanges.text: Three heads on one body. Caesar was in an arrangement like that once.

exchanges.speaker: cerberus
exchanges.text: [consults himself, three times over]

exchanges.speaker: death
exchanges.text: He asks how it ended.

exchanges.speaker: caesar
exchanges.text: With one head.
exchanges.note: The First Triumvirate: Caesar, Pompey and Crassus. Crassus died in Parthia; Caesar beat Pompey in the civil war.

exchanges.speaker: spartacus
exchanges.text: You and I both know chains, dog.

exchanges.speaker: cerberus
exchanges.text: [looks down at the chain that joins his three collars]

exchanges.speaker: death
exchanges.text: He says his was never locked. He simply never left.

exchanges.speaker: pope
exchanges.text: Good dog. Nice dog. Which of you is in charge?

exchanges.speaker: cerberus
exchanges.text: [all three heads turn slowly to look at one another]

exchanges.speaker: death
exchanges.text: They have been discussing that since Hesiod.

exchanges.speaker: caesar
exchanges.text: Caesar crossed the Rubicon. And what river do you keep?

exchanges.speaker: cerberus
exchanges.text: [licks his chops with all three tongues]

exchanges.speaker: death
exchanges.text: The last one. He would like you to know he has had emperors through it.

needles.speaker: cerberus
needles.text: [wags his serpent tail at the Pope, slowly]

needles.speaker: death
needles.text: He says the almond was not enough.

needles.speaker: cerberus
needles.text: [stands over the pot, three heads low, watching Spartacus]

needles.speaker: death
needles.text: He says everyone gets in. Nobody gets out.

needles.speaker: cerberus
needles.text: [pants happily at Caesar from all three mouths]

needles.speaker: death
needles.text: He likes you. He likes everyone who comes through his door, and in the end that is everyone.

needles.speaker: spartacus
needles.text: Down, dog.

needles.speaker: cerberus
needles.text: [lies down with one head; the other two refuse]

needles.speaker: pope
needles.text: You see? Even the hound of Hades can be reasoned with.

needles.speaker: death
needles.text: He folded because you smell of honey cake. He has not forgiven himself.

needles.speaker: caesar
needles.text: Three heads, and not one of them could hold.

needles.speaker: cerberus
needles.text: [puts his chins on the table and sulks, three times over]

tier_0.speaker: spartacus
tier_0.text: Fresh from the market. Nobody's even looked at your teeth yet.

tier_0.speaker: pope
tier_0.text: Sit, sit. Anywhere you like. No, not there. There.

tier_0.speaker: cerberus
tier_0.text: [sniffs at the player with two heads; the third cannot be bothered]

tier_0.speaker: spartacus
tier_0.text: Don't bother looking at the doors. I've already checked them.

tier_0.speaker: pope
tier_0.text: What a pleasure to meet someone of no importance. It is so rarely allowed me.

tier_1.speaker: spartacus
tier_1.text: Tiro. That's what the arena calls a fighter who hasn't had a bout yet. Keep this up and I'll stop calling you it.

tier_1.speaker: pope
tier_1.text: You are learning to smile when you lose. Good. That is most of what Rome can teach anyone.

tier_1.speaker: cerberus
tier_1.text: [turns his middle head to watch the player, and keeps watching]

tier_1.speaker: caesar
tier_1.text: Caesar has made a note of you. It is a short note.

tier_2.speaker: spartacus
tier_2.text: {name}. Good. A free person should be called by their own name.

tier_2.speaker: pope
tier_2.text: I have been asking about you. Nobody can tell me anything. I find that enormously attractive in a person.

tier_2.speaker: cerberus
tier_2.text: [lays one head on the table beside the player's chips]

tier_2.speaker: caesar
tier_2.text: Caesar remembers everyone who takes a pot from him. Ask the pirates.

tier_3.speaker: spartacus
tier_3.note: The soldiers' acclamation for a victorious general. Appian says Spartacus once served with the Romans; from the one man here who led an army against Rome, the word costs him something. Caesar arrives late, so the gladiator gets to say it first.

tier_3.speaker: caesar
tier_3.text: Caesar's soldiers hailed him Imperator. He had earned it. So have you.

tier_3.speaker: pope
tier_3.text: If you ever want a city, come and see me. I have given away several.

tier_3.speaker: cerberus
tier_3.text: [bows all three heads, very slightly, at the same moment]

death_asides.speaker: death
death_asides.text: Take as long as you like. Everyone else in this building has.

death_asides.speaker: death
death_asides.text: The Romans built temples to Fortune. She was not grateful then, either.

death_asides.speaker: death
death_asides.text: The night before the Ides, he told a dinner party the best death was an unexpected one. I have never liked being announced either.
death_asides.foreshadow: Reads as gallows wit about Caesar (Plutarch and Suetonius both record the dinner). It is also the dealer describing how he means to take his own seat at the end of the tour: unannounced.

death_asides.speaker: death
death_asides.text: In the old days, thumbs were involved at this point. Nobody now agrees which way they pointed.

death_asides.speaker: death
death_asides.text: Caesar called it casting the die. He was standing at a river at the time. People usually are.
death_asides.foreshadow: Reads as Rubicon trivia. The last table of the tour is a river crossing at night, and every all-in is a small rehearsal for it.

death_asides.speaker: death
death_asides.text: Two left. In Rome it always did come down to two.

death_asides.speaker: death
death_asides.text: The price of a seat goes up. Rome has never been cheap to sit in.

champion_arrival.speaker: narration
champion_arrival.text: The chair is still warm when the door opens. A man in a purple-bordered toga walks in dictating to a secretary, takes the laurel wreath from its cushion, puts it on, and sits.

champion_arrival.speaker: caesar
champion_arrival.text: A vacancy was reported. Caesar has filled it.
champion_arrival.note: Caesar's first words. Administrative, not grand: a seat became available.

champion_arrival.speaker: spartacus
champion_arrival.text: Of course. Rome always sends someone.
champion_arrival.note: Rome sent praetor after praetor against him, then both consuls, then Crassus. Works whether Spartacus is still seated or was the one just knocked out (then it is his parting shot). The dealer_plant follows.

champion_headsup.speaker: caesar
champion_headsup.note: Suetonius's words at the Rubicon. The die is cast; no translation needed.

champion_headsup.speaker: caesar
champion_headsup.text: The pirates asked twenty talents for me. I told them to ask fifty. Never let anyone set your price.

champion_headsup.speaker: caesar
champion_headsup.text: Better to die once than to spend a lifetime expecting it. Caesar bets the same way.
champion_headsup.note: Plutarch, Caesar 57: his answer when friends urged him to keep a bodyguard.

champion_headsup.speaker: caesar
champion_headsup.text: Enjoy it. The pirates enjoyed their thirty-eight days as well.

spartacus.speaker: spartacus
spartacus.text: Don't go looking for me afterwards. Last time, nobody found me.
spartacus.note: Appian: his body was never found.

spartacus.speaker: spartacus
spartacus.text: [rolls his neck, looks once at the doors, and walks out through them]

pope.speaker: pope
pope.text: Tell them I was poisoned. It will do the family less harm than the truth.

pope.speaker: pope
pope.text: [rises, gathers his robes, and congratulates the winner as though it had all been his idea]

cerberus.speaker: cerberus
cerberus.text: [lies down with all three heads at once, with enormous dignity]

cerberus.speaker: cerberus
cerberus.text: [whines from the left head; the other two pretend not to know it]

caesar.speaker: caesar
caesar.text: Unexpected. Good. Caesar always said that was the best kind.
caesar.note: Pays off ro_death_03 if it has fired; stands alone if it has not.

caesar.speaker: caesar
caesar.text: Put it in the commentaries: Caesar was beaten. In the third person. It reads better.

player_busted.speaker: spartacus
player_busted.text: Everyone goes down in their first fight. The ones worth watching get up.

player_busted.speaker: pope
player_busted.text: Come back when you have made some friends. It helps enormously, in Rome.

player_busted.speaker: death
player_busted.text: Come back whenever you like. The dog will let you in. That part he has never minded.

champion_defeat.speaker: caesar
champion_defeat.text: You came. You saw. Caesar leaves the third word to you.
champion_defeat.note: Veni, vidi, vici, with the last word handed to the player.

champion_defeat.speaker: death
champion_defeat.text: Five. Three remain. He has lost a room before. This one had fewer knives.
